title: Event 1
content:
Summary Report: “Buildrathon Kickoff: Code the Future with CMC Global” Event information Event Name: Buildrathon Kickoff: Code the Future with CMC Global
Date & Time: 09:00 a.m., September 26, 2026 (UTC+7)
Location: Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City
Role: Attendee
Event Page: Buildrathon Kickoff on Luma Event objectives Introduce Buildrathon, its objectives, and the direction for participants. Connect AWS Cloud and AI learning with practical perspectives from industry practitioners. Discuss the thinking behind AI applications through the talkshow The Thinking Behind Building the Bot. Give students opportunities to meet the community, hear from practitioners, and explore learning and career directions in Cloud and AI. Speakers Order Speaker Position Contribution to the event 1 Hung Gia Nguyen Head of Solutions Architect, AWS Vietnam and Cambodia Delivered the opening and introduced Buildrathon’s purpose and direction for participants. 2 Truong Nhat Bui Tech Lead, CMC Global Presented technical topics, including an AI-enabled Slack bot architecture, and responded to questions. 3 Thien Lu Program Manager, FCAJ Participated as a speaker representing the FCAJ program. The introduction helped me understand the context of Buildrathon. The technical session then connected the discussion to an application example, making it easier to relate the event to my studies.
Key highlights Program introduction and Buildrathon orientation Hung Gia Nguyen opened the program and explained the purpose of Buildrathon. The introduction helped attendees see how Cloud and AI learning can connect with building a product. For me, this raised a question to answer before choosing an internship project, namely who the product will help and which need it will address. The Thinking Behind Building the Bot talkshow Truong Nhat Bui shared technical perspectives and introduced an architecture example for a Slack bot with AI capabilities. The example gave me a concrete reference for thinking about application structure, from receiving a request to processing it and returning a result. I want to explore each component’s responsibilities and how the components work together before trying to build a bot myself. Discussion with the speaker The question-and-answer discussion gave attendees an opportunity to clarify points from the presentation. I participated as a listener, followed the discussion, and related the topics to my AWS learning. Areas that require more study will guide my further reading and the questions I prepare for conversations with my mentor. Key takeaways Product thinking Identify the intended users and their needs before selecting technology. Keep the scope appropriate for the available time and my ability to implement it. Define verifiable outcomes so that I can assess whether an exercise meets its objectives. Approaching architecture Break a system into components with clear responsibilities. Follow the data flow to understand how those components work together. Practice explaining design choices and how to check each step in a workflow. Learning skills Record interesting points and unresolved questions after a presentation. Combine reading with a small exercise that has a clear objective. Participate in the community to encounter different perspectives on work and technology. Applying to work Prepare my personal workshop. I plan to choose a small problem, describe its users, and identify its main functionality. Outline the architecture. I will define the inputs, outputs, and workflow before considering AWS services. Explore AI applications. I want to study how to provide context and evaluate a bot’s answers. Update my worklog. I will record technical decisions, experiment results, and errors encountered during my studies. Event experience The kickoff was a memorable experience early in my internship. Hearing the presentations in person at the AWS office motivated me to explore Cloud and AI and think more concretely about my own practical learning.
Learning from industry practitioners Heard the program’s direction from AWS and FCAJ representatives. Followed the technical presentation from the CMC Global representative. Connected the topics with choosing a project and planning my learning during the internship. Participating with the community Attended the event and kept a check-in photo. Took a group photo with others. Experienced a learning environment connecting students, the community, and industry practitioners. The hands-on AI Agent Challenge listed in the published agenda did not take place during this event. My participation focused on listening to the presentations and following the discussion.

title: Event 2
content:
Summary Report: “AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi - Watch Party” Event information Event Name: AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi - Watch Party
Date & Time: 08:00 a.m. to 05:00 p.m., Tuesday, September 29, 2026 (UTC+7), according to the published schedule
Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Ho Chi Minh City. Badge collection on the 26th floor, as stated in the invitation.
Attendance Format: Watch party in Ho Chi Minh City, following sessions broadcast from the main event in Hanoi
Role: Attendee
Event Page: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi On September 29, I attended the watch party at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City with my teammates. The main event took place in Hanoi, and we followed the keynote and technical sessions on screens at the office. The topics I wanted to keep from the day concerned using AI in software development, from preparing work for an agent to checking its results and securing an application.
Event objectives Introduce Cloud and AI use cases through presentations from AWS and businesses. Share approaches to using agentic AI in software development, testing, and operations. Allow the community in Ho Chi Minh City to follow the keynote and selected Builders x AI sessions from Hanoi together. My aim was to find approaches I could try on a small scale while studying and preparing my personal workshop.
Speakers The table records selected speakers from the keynote and security session broadcast from Hanoi.
Order Speaker Position Presentation topics 1 Eric Yeo Country General Manager, Malaysia, Vietnam & Indochina, AWS Cloud and AI adoption in Vietnam, with examples from businesses. 2 Werner Vogels CTO, Amazon Engineering decisions behind cloud services, including databases, compute infrastructure, and time synchronization. 3 Jens Lottner CEO, Techcombank Bringing AI into banking operations and preparing employees to work with it. 4 Mai Le Director of Product Management, Katalon Software validation during development with AI and human responsibility for the results. 5 Trung Nguyen Technical Account Manager, AWS Vietnam Joint presentation of AWS Security Agent: Proactive AppSec from Design to Deployment. 6 Tan Huynh Technical Account Manager, AWS Vietnam Joint presentation of AWS Security Agent and the security testing workflow. 7 Hoàng Minh Deputy Minister of Science and Technology Opening remarks at the event. 8 Jennifer Wicks U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam Technology cooperation, digital infrastructure, and workforce development. Key highlights Opening and AI adoption in Vietnam Eric Yeo opened the program, introduced the guests and speakers, and thanked the event partners. Deputy Minister Hoàng Minh and Ambassador Jennifer Wicks then delivered their remarks. Jennifer Wicks discussed the role of cloud computing in business, technology cooperation between Vietnam and the United States, and the development of infrastructure and workforce skills.
Returning to the stage, Eric Yeo spoke about AWS’s twentieth anniversary and the AWS Local Zone in Hanoi. He introduced examples from several industries: OmiGroup’s research into chronic diseases with links to medical evidence, Vinasoy’s monitoring of retail product displays, and Agris’s use of data across agricultural operations. These examples helped me understand the specific problems each business wanted to address with Cloud and AI.
Techcombank: preparing the platform and people to use AI Jens Lottner explained how Techcombank organizes AI adoption. Building on its existing data foundation and AWS services, the bank added a platform for coordinating agents, workflows, access permissions, and controls. Employees can use prepared agents or build workflows suited to their own tasks.
One example that caught my attention was AI Coach, which helps employees select models, write requests, and consider usage costs. The presentation also covered training at different skill levels so employees can use and operate these tools.
Three areas of application were introduced: software development, incident coordination, and support for staff working with customers. In the incident example, an agent coordinates information between operations and customer-facing teams so remediation and customer updates can proceed together. At the end of his presentation, Jens Lottner discussed cost, return on investment, talent, and risk management. These are questions I also need to consider when choosing a problem to explore with AI.
The FCAJ community and a greeting to Ho Chi Minh City Eric Yeo continued with AWS training activities, First Cloud and AI Journey, and AWS Academy. He shared stories of people who started learning cloud, secured internships, and returned to support the community. This part related closely to my own internship, where learning needs practical work and opportunities to speak with more experienced people.
Before inviting Werner Vogels onto the stage, Eric Yeo greeted the community watching the livestream in Ho Chi Minh City. I wanted to record this moment because my team was attending at that location.
Werner Vogels: the engineering behind cloud services Werner Vogels recalled a database incident during a peak shopping period at Amazon. By reviewing how applications accessed their data, the team found that many needs could be served by a key-value model. His example of retrieving a shopping cart by customer ID helped me understand why actual query patterns matter when choosing a database.
He then presented three stories about improvements behind the services:
AWS Nitro: Moving much of the I/O work to dedicated hardware reduces the burden on the hypervisor and improves isolation. This example showed how an infrastructure change can affect both performance and security. Lambda, Firecracker, and SnapStart: Starting with the need to process a file uploaded to S3, the presentation explored running small functions with suitable isolation and cost. Firecracker was introduced through its microVM approach, while SnapStart was explained through saving initialized state to reduce startup time. Time synchronization: He described the difficulty of ordering events across multiple machines and how AWS provides accurate time with explicit error bounds. I want to study this further when learning about data and distributed systems. These examples made the work behind familiar actions, such as creating a virtual machine or running a Lambda function, easier to understand. When studying a service, I need to understand the problem it solves and the conditions that affect its use.
Katalon: validating software as AI generates code faster Mai Le began with a familiar coding-agent interaction: the user points out an error, and the agent agrees to correct it. She used this to introduce the gap between the speed of software creation and the capacity to validate it. When testing falls behind, errors can reach end users.
The presentation described connecting requirements, code changes, tests, execution results, defects, and production data to assess a release. Agents need this context to identify changes, select what to test, run the tests, and gather evidence. People remain responsible for setting risk boundaries, reviewing exceptions, and approving releases.
Mai Le also described the roles of Amazon EKS, RDS, S3, and Kinesis in Katalon’s platform, alongside Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore Runtime for its AI capabilities. The point I want to apply to my own work is to keep actual verification results, such as logs, screenshots, and test outcomes, so I can explain why a feature meets its requirements.
To close the keynote, Werner Vogels returned to the validation work that can accumulate as more code is generated, and to engineers’ professional responsibility. He spoke about work that users rarely see but that still requires care. I connected this with error handling, testing, and resource cleanup in my own workshop.
AI-DLC and how TCBS organizes work for agents I kept photos of the comparison between traditional SDLC and AI-DLC, along with the workspace diagram from TCBS. In the diagram, an orchestrator prepares and monitors workspaces for individual agents and tasks. Each workspace includes a task package, source code, MCP tools, verification steps, and a checkpoint.
What I want to learn from this example is how to prepare a task before assigning it to AI. If the requirement and completion criteria are unclear, it is also difficult for me to judge the result. I can start by defining the inputs, outputs, and checks for each small feature in my workshop.
AWS Security Agent and security testing during development Session DVT305, presented by Trung Nguyen and Tan Huynh, covered application security from design through deployment. One slide outlined a workflow involving login, scanning, execution of testing tasks, further exploration based on findings, and resource cleanup.
This made me pay closer attention to the scope of a test: which system is being tested, what permissions are needed, and which resources must be removed afterward. These are also details I need to explain clearly in an AWS workshop. The session gave me subjects to explore, while applying them will require reading the documentation and practicing each step.
Agent Toolkit for AWS and MCP The Agent Toolkit for AWS slides introduced ways to give coding agents tools, knowledge, and controls. The getting started sequence covered installing a plugin, checking the connection to the AWS MCP Server, and trying a specific request. I also photographed the slide containing QR codes for the source repository and further reading.
I am interested in where an agent gets its information and which actions it can perform. When I try these tools after the event, I want to begin with a small task, read the changes it produces, and check the outcome before expanding the scope.
Key takeaways Prepare the requirement before using AI Divide work into tasks with clear outputs. Provide source code, documentation, and constraints relevant to the task. Decide how to check the result before starting. Take responsibility for the result Read and understand changes proposed by AI before including them in my work. Test successful behavior and error cases. Keep practice results so I can explain my decisions. Choose an approach based on the actual problem Understand how data will be read and written before choosing a database. When trying AI, consider usage costs, access permissions, and the time needed to check results. Make time to learn the tools and assess their output, as illustrated by the employee training in Techcombank’s presentation. Include security in the practice plan Review permissions and resource scope before running a tool. Include verification and cleanup steps in the workshop instructions. Learn the limits of tools, especially those able to act on an AWS environment. Applying to work I plan to begin with my personal workshop. For each feature, I will write a short requirement, identify the expected outcome, and define a check before asking AI for help. I will then review the changes, run the exercise, and record the results in my worklog.
For MCP and Agent Toolkit for AWS, I want to try a task in a practice environment with a defined scope. I will record the setup, any problems encountered, and the checks I complete after trying it.
Following the keynote, I also want to add a short explanation of data access patterns and service choices to my workshop design. For each feature change, I will retain the original requirement, the changes made, and verification evidence to refer to when preparing my report or demo.
Event experience Following the program with my team in Ho Chi Minh City The watch party let me follow the program with my teammates at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City. Our photo collection includes a group picture with attendance badges and photos of technical sessions on screen. Looking back through them helps me connect each point in this report to a specific presentation.
What I want to explore next The TCBS workspace diagram is an example I want to revisit when dividing up project work. The testing and security sessions also reminded me to make time for checks after writing code. My next step is to choose a small part to try, record the results, and then decide whether it belongs in my workshop.
Some event photos These images come from my team’s and my own attendance photo collection in Ho Chi Minh City. The slides belong to their presenters and organizations and were photographed from screens showing the program from Hanoi.

title: Week 3 Worklog

title: Event 3
content:
Summary Report: “Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels” Event information Event Name: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels
Date & Time: 08:30 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., Friday, October 2, 2026 (UTC+7)
Location: AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City
Attendance Format: In person
Role: Attendee
Just a few days earlier, I had watched Dr. Werner Vogels’ keynote on a screen at the AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi watch party. On October 2, I had the opportunity to hear him in person at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City. As someone studying Cloud and starting an internship, meeting Amazon’s CTO was an honor and a memorable experience.
Attendance objectives Hear Dr. Werner Vogels’ experience of building and operating systems at scale. Explore perspectives on Cloud, AI, and the skills needed in engineering. Connect what I learned with preparing my workshop and studying during the internship. Attend a community conversation in person with other AWS learners and practitioners in Ho Chi Minh City. Speakers Order Speaker Position 1 Dr. Werner Vogels VP and Chief Technology Officer, Amazon 2 Hung Gia Nguyen Head of Solutions Architect, AWS Vietnam and Cambodia 3 My Nguyen Solutions Architect, AWS Vietnam Topics and reflections after the event Hearing directly from an experienced practitioner The Fireside Chat centered on Cloud, AI, technology innovation, and experience building systems at scale. I attended as a learner, hoping to understand how someone with extensive experience approaches problems I am only beginning to explore.
What I wanted to take away was a clearer direction for my studies. Alongside learning how to use AWS services, I need to explain why I choose a service, which need it serves, and what could happen when something fails. These questions give me a starting point for further reading and practice.
Seeing a feature as part of a system I want to understand how the parts of an application depend on one another. A change to data storage or request processing can affect other parts of the system, so I need to consider those connections when making a design decision.
For my personal workshop, I want to trace a request from start to finish. Where does the data arrive, how is it processed, where is it stored, and how is the result returned? If one step fails, how does it affect the others? Drawing this flow will help me understand my work and explain it more clearly.
Taking responsibility when using AI I am responsible for the code I use, including code suggested by AI. I can ask a tool for an approach or an explanation of an error, but I need to review and check its output before including it in my own work.
I want to develop the habit of explaining the code I use. When I do not understand a piece of logic, I will study it further, run it, and check error cases. This should also help me recognize gaps in my knowledge.
Developing depth and communicating with others At this stage of my internship, I need to spend time on AWS fundamentals while learning how applications, data, and security fit together. I also need to practice explaining my work so that others can understand my choices and give useful feedback.
When working with my team or speaking with a mentor, I want to describe a problem in a way that is easy to follow: the goal, what I tried, the result, and where I am stuck. Preparing that information should make the discussion more specific and useful.
Key takeaways Understand before choosing: Start with the need and workflow, then choose the technology. Check error cases: Once a feature works, examine how it responds to missing data or a failed processing step. Take responsibility for my work: Review, test, and explain the parts developed with AI assistance. Keep learning regularly: Choose something I do not yet understand, practice it, and record the result. Communicate clearly: Describe the goal, completed work, and help needed when working with others. Applying to work While preparing my workshop, I plan to draw the data flow and briefly explain why I chose each AWS service. For every feature, I will prepare a successful case and an error case to test.
When using AI assistance, I will keep the original requirement, review the changes, and run them before adding them to the instructions. I will record technical decisions, errors, and solutions in my worklog so I can revisit them.
I also want to practice explaining my work to teammates. If I struggle to explain a component or a choice, that will identify an area to study before completing the demo.
Event experience A memorable opportunity during my internship Meeting Dr. Werner Vogels in person made this event particularly meaningful to me. As an attendee, I had the opportunity to hear from someone with many years of experience in Cloud and large distributed systems. It gave me more motivation to continue studying this field.
I appreciate the time he took to visit the AWS office and share his experience with the community. For me, a practical way to respond to that opportunity is to take my studies and project work seriously, starting with small tasks that I can understand, test, and explain myself.
Some event photos Figure 1. My photo in the audience at the Fireside Chat on October 2, 2026.
Figure 2. The conversation at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City. Both images come from my personal event photo collection.
References Le Vu Xuan An, AWS Builder Center, October 3, 2026: The Invariable Lessons of Tech and Humanity: Key Takeaways from Amazon CTO Werner Vogels .
